source.title: When To Solve, When To Verify: Compute-Optimal Problem Solving and Generative Verification for LLM Reasoning
source.authors: Nishad Singhi; Hritik Bansal; Arian Hosseini; Aditya Grover; Kai-Wei Chang; Marcus Rohrbach; A. Rohrbach

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted appendix prompt and example text has formatting noise.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies test-time compute allocation, not pretraining loss scaling. It explicitly adapts the compute-optimal fitting approach associated with Chinchilla to solution and verification counts, without testing the claimed pretraining laws.
record.gate_note: The reported Self-Consistency versus GenRM success-rate comparisons concern inference strategies, not held-out pretraining loss, model/token training scaling, or downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss; they are not rows for these versions. The paper does report power-law fits for compute-optimal inference-time solution and verification counts; these are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study scales inference-time compute (solutions vs. verifications) for fixed pretrained models and borrows the Chinchilla fitting procedure as a tool. It reports no pretraining loss, no variation in parameters or training tokens, and no downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss, so its results do not bear on V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct but incomplete. The authors' headline finding is that Self-Consistency beats GenRM at most practical inference budgets: GenRM needs up to 8× compute to match SC and far more to surpass it. This holds across model families, sizes, a thinking model and tasks. They also derive inference scaling laws in which optimal solutions should grow 1.5–2× faster than verifications.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits inference-time success-rate allocations between solution samples and verifications, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss against parameters, training tokens, or training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted inference-allocation exponents vary across the tested model and verifier configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: On MATH, the compute-optimal inference-time counts of solutions and verifications were fitted as power laws in inference compute. Solutions scale faster: Llama-8B GenRM-FT C^0.57 vs C^0.39; Qwen-7B GenRM-FT C^0.75 vs C^0.32; Llama-70B GenRM-Base C^0.69 vs C^0.43.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For GenRM best-of-N inference, compute-optimal solution and verification counts each scale roughly as a power of inference compute, with solutions scaling about 1.5–2× faster.

record.problems: The study does not test the pretraining-loss scaling claim. For its related inference-time fits, it reports no uncertainty for the fitted exponents and bases its analysis on sampled, finite ranges of solution and verification counts.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the claim versions. Success-rate comparisons between SC and GenRM across inference budgets are described in Sections 5.1 and Appendices E–I, but they measure inference-strategy performance rather than a version of the pretraining scaling claim.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; not measured.
Extrapolation from small to large pretraining runs; not measured.
Compute-optimal split of parameters and training tokens; the study's split is between inference solutions and verifications, not training resources.
Architecture shape effects at fixed parameter count; not measured.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes; the inference-time allocation fits are a different construct.
Downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss; 8B vs 70B comparisons concern the SC vs GenRM crossover, not scale-performance trends.
Fit-dependence of pretraining-law exponents or splits; not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The rows themselves are correctly linked to none. Exponents come from fits over narrow, discrete ranges (at most 2^7 solutions or verifications) with no uncertainty reported. The section 5.2 text describes Figure 6 as 'Llama-3-8B' while the setup uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Kaplan et al. is cited only for the 2P FLOPs-per-token rule, and Hoffmann et al. only for the fitting procedure.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, and training compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of model parameters and training tokens under a fixed training-compute budget.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss; the paper instead reports reasoning-task performance under test-time compute scaling.
Dependence or disagreement of pretraining scaling-law fits and training compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.

relation.reason: Uses the Chinchilla approach to fit optimal solution and verification counts against inference compute, without testing V1–V7.

tranche.reason: Section 3.2 adapts Chinchilla's fitting procedure to inference allocation. The results do not test the specified loss, training-allocation, architecture, or downstream model-scale claims.

source_check.notes: All six exponents are explicitly stated with the recorded models and conditions. Their links to no claim version and the absence of verdicts are appropriate; the state corrections concern catalog claim evidence.
